People imagine that I read every CV carefully. I wish I could. For most positions, we receive hundreds of applications. So first, the CVs are screened by software. It looks for the words in the job posting. If the posting says advanced English and your CV doesn't mention English at all, you're out, even if you speak it perfectly. The ones that make it through come to me, and honestly, I spend about thirty seconds on each one at first. And here's a little secret. When a candidate says fluent, I call them, and I start the conversation in English, without warning. It's amazing how many people panic.

The biggest mistake I see on CVs is the word fluent. Everybody is fluent, apparently. Then they get to the interview, and the recruiter discovers the truth in two minutes. My advice is to be honest and specific. Describe each skill separately. Proficient in reading and writing. Brushing up on spoken English. Then add proof: a certificate, a project you did in English, a client you worked with. It is often said that honesty is a soft skill, and in recruitment it really is. The interview will show the truth anyway. And recruiters trust candidates who know their own level.

My team is spread across four countries, so everybody works in English. When a CV gets to me, I look at the track record first. Not the adjectives, the facts. What did you actually do? Then, in the interview, I'm looking for soft skills. And the one I value most is surprisingly simple. Can you say I don't know, and then ask a good question? People who can do that in a second language are gold. And about accents, I'm often asked if a strong accent is a problem. It isn't. I have colleagues from Brazil, India and Germany. What matters is being clear, being natural, and being yourself.
